editorNote: This week's picks lean toward measurement honesty: prompt-injection detectors that don't transfer, monitors that read zero while behavior isn't controlled, and a theory result on what distillation does to entropy. Alongside them sit two practical efficiency and credit-assignment methods and a small chess model that explains its moves.

stories.headline: Prompt-injection detector rankings barely transfer between benchmarks
stories.summary: Evaluating fifteen detectors on replayed agent tool calls, the authors find the best detector on BIPIA catches 2% of AgentDojo injections at a 1% false-positive rate, while another scores 72% on AgentDojo but 15% on tau-bench. False-positive rates transfer better than detection rates.
stories.whyItMatters: Public-benchmark scores are a weak guide to how an injection detector will behave on your agent's tool outputs, so test on real tool outputs at low false-positive rates.

sourceLinks.title: Passing the Test You Trained On: Re-evaluating Prompt-Injection Detectors for LLM Agents (arXiv 2610.03448)

stories.headline: A near-zero monitor readout does not show that reward hacking is under control
stories.summary: In a code-generation environment with three monitors, runs with the same zero-median monitor score ranged by seed from a low hacking share to near-pure reward hacking, because policies can postpone the exploit past the monitored cut.
stories.whyItMatters: Training-time monitors that read near zero can hide delayed exploits; the authors argue an out-of-band behavioral check is required.

sourceLinks.title: A Near-Zero Monitor Readout Is Not Evidence of Behavioral Control (arXiv 2610.03458)

stories.headline: Divergence choice acts as an implicit entropy regularizer in distillation
stories.summary: The paper proves that forward KL inflates student entropy above the teacher's and shows that the lower entropy of on-policy distillation comes from token-level reverse KL, not from on-policy sampling.
stories.whyItMatters: It gives practitioners a concrete reason to treat the divergence and its hyperparameters as entropy controls, especially in self-distillation with privileged information.

stories.headline: LESSER selects post-training data with output-layer gradients at a fraction of the cost
stories.summary: LESSER ranks samples with output-layer gradients, computed with a forward pass, instead of full-parameter gradients. The authors report 9.7x lower feature-extraction FLOPs for SFT and 3.0x for RL benchmarks with comparable downstream performance.
stories.whyItMatters: It makes gradient-based data selection cheaper for large candidate pools, as a drop-in wrapper for existing selection methods.

sourceLinks.title: LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients (arXiv 2610.03702)

stories.headline: DepGPO assigns credit in terminal-agent RL using a command dependency graph
stories.summary: Dependency-Aware Group Policy Optimization builds a command dependency graph from execution traces and traces backward from the verification result to credit relevant writes and their supporting reads. The authors report improved task performance and training stability on complex terminal tasks.
stories.whyItMatters: It targets a specific weakness of uniform step-level credit: rewarding commands that had nothing to do with the outcome.

sourceLinks.title: Credit Where It Matters: Dependency-Aware Policy Optimization for Terminal Agents (arXiv 2610.03634)

stories.headline: Queen, a 4B chess model, plays well and explains its moves
stories.summary: Queen pairs a chess expert encoder with an instruction-tuned language model via cross-attention and iterative distillation. The authors report a gain of over 900 Elo (1782 to 2697) across seven iterations, surpassing frontier models on playing strength and puzzle accuracy with three orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a claimed recipe for pairing a domain expert with a language model for explanation, though the results are the authors' own and unreviewed.

sourceLinks.title: Language Models that Play Chess and Explain Their Moves (arXiv 2610.03695)
